title: Dissociation Mechanisms
subtitle: Disrupted integration of awareness, memory, identity or perception
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating dissociation mechanisms across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain dissociation mechanisms in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in dissociation mechanisms.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to dissociation mechanisms.

sections.explainSimply: Dissociation can involve detachment, altered awareness, memory discontinuity or compartmentalised responding.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Mechanisms likely vary across depersonalisation, derealisation, amnesia and identity disturbance rather than reflecting one neural state.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Studies implicate altered frontolimbic, salience and sensory integration, but findings are heterogeneous and strongly state-dependent.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of dissociation mechanisms as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need dissociation mechanisms to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not infer dissociation from a scan or reduced arousal alone.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use dissociation mechanisms to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses dissociation mechanisms to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not infer dissociation from a scan or reduced arousal alone. Evidence classification: mixed neurobiological evidence.
